query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Hf to the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will prevent radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication under energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service.
generation.structural_mediator: high density of stable grain boundaries, chemical complexity altering defect recombination rates
generation.mechanism: decrease in the order-disorder transition temperature (ODTT), stabilization of the solid solution based on simple underlying BCC crystal structure
generation.predicted_outcome: prevention of radiation-induced precipitation, retention of negligible irradiation hardening, improvement in suitability for practical bulk fabrication
generation.boundary: irradiation dose: approximately 8 dpa, temperature range: reactor-relevant temperatures
generation.uncertainty: effect of Hf addition on the alloy's microstructure and properties under different irradiation conditions and temperatures

falsification_experiment.design: compare the microstructure and properties of the Hf-modified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy with the unmodified alloy under energetic-particle irradiation at approximately 8 dpa
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the Hf-modified alloy exhibits significant radiation-induced precipitation or increased hardening, the hypothesis is falsified

In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. The aim of such design is to develop a RHEA with higher irradiation resistance, high thermal stability, enhanced control over the morphology, and no precipitation at reactor-relevant temperatures. By using a combination of (i) thermophysical parameter calculations including minimizing the valence electron concentration (VEC) which was shown to enhance the mechanical performance of HEAs,, (ii) the CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) method with its newest high-entropy alloy database, and (iii) Cluster Expansion (CE) along with Monte Carlo calculations to predict the alloy’s morphology, a methodology to foster the discovery of novel RHEAs for application in extreme environments is proposed. ## Results
The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆Hmix), entropy of mixing (ΔSmix), atomic size difference (δ), and the omega parameter (Ω) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for ΔHmix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1,. ∆Hmix, δ, and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1–4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density (ρ), melting temperature (Tm), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5, where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i.
The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. ,, respectively. The base material for this design was the W-Ta-Cr-V HEA which shows high mechanical strength and radiation resistance to loop and He bubble formation under ion irradiation. As mentioned in the methods section, two films were prepared: (1) 100 nm thin film to study the thermal stability and the irradiation response to He implantation and dual-beam irradiation, and (2) a 3 µm film for morphology and hardness analysis via APT and nanoindentation, respectively. The deposited thin and thick (bulk) films with Hf had compositions of W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 and W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 which are predicted by CALPHAD to form a single-phase BCC structure over a wide temperature range (illustrated in the supplementary). We acknowledge that both films have different compositions, which is due to challenges in depositing specific compositions from five different targets within this quinary system.
